chief_complaint: severe coughing spells waking me up at night and tight chest during morning jogs for 3 months
hpi_details: 3-month history of frequent, troublesome dry coughing fits that characteristically wake her from sleep between 2 AM and 4 AM at least three times a week. During the day, experiences recurrent tightness across her chest and audible wheezing whenever she goes for morning runs in cold autumn air or cleans her dusty attic. Her symptoms improved slightly while on a 2-week beach vacation last month but flared up immediately upon returning home to her two pet cats. Denies fever, purulent sputum, weight loss, or heartburn.
ideas: thinks she has developed a chronic dust allergy or sensitivity to her cats' dander that clogs her breathing tubes
concerns: worried that a severe coughing attack at night will restrict her airway completely while sleeping
expectations: wants allergy testing and a daily preventer inhaler to open her airways and stop the night cough
pmh: childhood eczema, allergic rhinitis (hay fever) every spring, mother has asthma
medications: over-the-counter cetirizine 10mg OD for hay fever with partial relief of nasal symptoms
social_hx: non-smoker, zero alcohol, high school science teacher, lives with husband and two indoor cats

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bronchial Asthma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Controller and reliever therapy is selected by a clinician using current guideline recommendations, symptom control, exacerbation risk, objective testing, and patient preferences.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe coughing spells waking me up at night and tight chest during morning jogs for 3 months

Key HPI features: 3-month history of frequent, troublesome dry coughing fits that characteristically wake her from sleep between 2 AM and 4 AM at least three times a week. During the day, experiences recurrent tightness across her chest and audible wheezing whenever she goes for morning runs in cold autumn air or cleans her dusty attic. Her symptoms improved slightly while on a 2-week beach vacation last month but flared up immediately upon returning home to her two pet cats. Denies fever, purulent sputum, weight loss, or heartburn.

Objective/Exam findings: Respiratory exam in clinic during asymptomatic period: auscultation may be completely normal (normal lung exam does NOT exclude asthma), or show mild end-expiratory polyphonic wheeze on forced expiration. Perform objective lung function testing: Spirometry: demonstrates obstructive pattern with reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio ( positive diagnostic reversibility confirmed by an increase in FEV1 of >=12% and >=200 mL. Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) home diary monitoring: shows significant diurnal variability (>20% difference between morning and evening readings over 2 weeks). Bloods: peripheral blood eosinophilia (>0.4 x 10^9/L), elevated total IgE and specific IgE RAST tests for cat dander/house dust mite. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): markedly elevated (>40 parts per billion confirming active Type 2 / eosinophilic airway inflammation).
Relevant background/PMH: childhood eczema, allergic rhinitis (hay fever) every spring, mother has asthma
Current medications: over-the-counter cetirizine 10mg OD for hay fever with partial relief of nasal symptoms
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Bronchial Asthma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vocal cord dysfunction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Silent chest (absent breath sounds during severe attack).
management_principles: Use a clinician-directed inhaled anti-inflammatory and reliever regimen after confirming the diagnosis and assessing severity.
Explain clearly that the steroid component treats chronic airway inflammation while formoterol provides rapid and sustained bronchodilation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 42F atopic female presents with 3-month classical triad of nocturnal dry cough waking at 2-4 AM, exertional/cold-air wheezing, and allergen-induced chest tightness (cats/dust).
reference_soap.objective: Respiratory exam in clinic during asymptomatic period: auscultation may be completely normal (normal lung exam does NOT exclude asthma), or show mild end-expiratory polyphonic wheeze on forced expiration. Perform objective lung function testing: Spirometry: demonstrates obstructive pattern with reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.70). Perform Bronchodilator Reversibility Test: administer 400mcg inhaled salbutamol and repeat spirometry after 15 minutes -> positive diagnostic reversibility confirmed by an increase in FEV1 of >=12% and >=200 mL. Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) home diary monitoring: shows significant diurnal variability (>20% difference between morning and evening readings over 2 weeks). Bloods: peripheral blood eosinophilia (>0.4 x 10^9/L), elevated total IgE and specific IgE RAST tests for cat dander/house dust mite. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): markedly elevated (>40 parts per billion confirming active Type 2 / eosinophilic airway inflammation).
reference_soap.assessment: Adult-Onset Atopic Bronchial Asthma (Eosinophilic Type 2 phenotype). DDx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD causing nocturnal micro-aspiration cough without diurnal PEFR variability), cough-variant asthma, post-nasal drip / upper airway cough syndrome, vocal cord dysfunction.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm variable airflow limitation where feasible and review inhaler technique, triggers, and comorbid allergic rhinitis. Agree a clinician-directed anti-inflammatory and reliever regimen with a written action plan and follow-up. Seek emergency care for severe breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis, a silent chest, low oxygen saturation, or poor response to the prescribed reliever.

learning_objectives: Identify the pathognomonic clinical features of bronchial asthma: nocturnal cough/wheeze waking between 2-4 AM, exercise/cold provocation, and atopic history
Perform and interpret diagnostic spirometry reversibility criteria (>=12% and >=200 mL FEV1 improvement post-salbutamol) and FeNO (>40 ppb)
Prescribe first-line MART (Maintenance And Reliever Therapy) using low-dose ICS-formoterol combination inhalers
Formulate an empowering, structured written Asthma Action Plan tied to Peak Flow Rate monitoring and environmental allergen control

teaching.one_liner: Chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
red_flags: Silent chest (absent breath sounds during severe attack)
Pulsus paradoxus, inability to speak full sentences, or poor response to prescribed reliever therapy
Hypoxemia, cyanosis, or rapidly worsening breathlessness

must_ask.say: Do you hear a high-pitched whistling sound when you breathe out or feel chest tightness?
Are your coughing and wheezing attacks worse late at night or early in the morning?
Do cold air, exercise, pollen, dust mites, or pet dander trigger your breathlessness?
Do you or your family members have allergic rhinitis, hay fever, or eczema?
How quickly does your blue rescue inhaler open up your chest during an attack?

history.answer: I have been having terrible coughing fits that wake me up in the middle of the night, and my chest feels tight when I go jogging.
It has been going on for about three months now and seems to be getting more frequent.
It started gradually this autumn without an obvious cold or flu, though I had a similar mild chest tightness during springtime runs last year.
It is purely a dry cough. I am not coughing up any phlegm or yellow mucus at all.
It is definitely worst in the dead of night, waking me up between 2 AM and 4 AM at least three times every week. It does not bother me just from lying flat in bed.
They come as sudden, severe coughing spells that leave me breathless, but I do not make a whooping gasp and I have never thrown up from coughing.
It flares up whenever I jog in the cold morning air, clean our dusty attic, or spend time around my cats. It actually improved during a two-week beach vacation last month.
Yes, I hear an audible whistling or wheezing sound in my chest and feel a tight band around it when I jog or clean the house.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweats.
No, there has never been any blood in my cough.
My weight has been completely steady and I do not get night sweats.
My chest feels tight and constricted when I cough or exert myself, but there is no sharp stabbing pain when I take a deep breath.
I get seasonal runny nose and sneezing every spring, which cetirizine helps with, but right now I do not feel mucus dripping down the back of my throat.
No, I do not suffer from heartburn, sour fluid coming up, or frequent throat clearing.
No, I do not get short of breath from lying flat, and my ankles are not swollen.
I do not take any high blood pressure medication or any prescription pills.
No, no one at home or in my school has had a chronic cough or illness.
I have never had tuberculosis and I have never been in contact with anyone who had it.
I teach science at a high school with no heavy fumes or industrial dust, but my attic is very dusty and I have two indoor cats.
I had eczema when I was a child, and I get bad hay fever every spring.
I have never tried an asthma inhaler because no doctor has ever prescribed one for me.
I think I have developed a chronic allergy to dust or my cats' fur that is clogging up my airways.
I am really terrified that one night my chest will tighten up completely and choke me in my sleep.
I am hoping to get proper allergy testing and maybe an inhaler to open my airways and stop these night attacks.
Aside from childhood eczema and seasonal allergic rhinitis, I have always been healthy.
I have never had surgery and I have never been hospitalized.
I take over-the-counter cetirizine 10 milligrams once a day for my allergies, and nothing else.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products in my life.
I do not drink any alcohol.
I teach high school science and live in a house with my husband and two indoor cats.
My mother has asthma and my father has high blood pressure.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago. My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Nasal mucosa appears mildly boggy and pale; oropharynx is clear without erythema, exudates, or posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy noted bilaterally.
Symmetric chest expansion with no accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, or chest wall tenderness; normal tactile fremitus.
Resonant to percussion across all bilateral lung fields without focal dullness.
Vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with mild end-expiratory polyphonic wheezing audible on forced expiration; no crackles or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
No peripheral edema in lower extremities bilaterally, and no digital clubbing or peripheral cyanosis.
